words.definition: To confirm or give support to a claim with additional evidence or testimony.
words.example: Two other witnesses corroborated her account of exactly what happened that night.
words.mnemonic: Co- (together) + robor- (Latin robur, 'strength'): together you make a story stronger.

words.definition: To prove the truth of something by providing solid evidence.
words.example: The reporter could not substantiate the rumor, so the editor killed the story.
words.mnemonic: You add real 'substance' to a claim, turning hot air into hard proof.

words.definition: To prove that a statement or argument is wrong or false.
words.example: She used lab data to refute the theory that the drug was harmless.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'refuse' — you refuse to accept the claim by proving it false.

words.definition: To argue against a claim by offering opposing reasons or evidence.
words.example: The defense attorney rose to rebut the prosecutor's closing argument point by point.
words.mnemonic: Re-BUTT: you butt heads right back against the other side's argument.

words.definition: To reject or refuse to accept or be associated with something.
words.example: The senator publicly repudiated the extremist group that had endorsed his campaign.
words.mnemonic: Re-PU! — 'pew, that stinks' — so you push it away and disown it.

words.definition: To clear someone of blame, or to show that a decision was right.
words.example: The new DNA evidence finally vindicated the man who had spent years in prison.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'win-dicate': you WIN your good name back and are cleared.

words.definition: To check or confirm that something is correct, sound, or officially acceptable.
words.example: Please validate your parking ticket at the front desk before you leave the garage.
words.mnemonic: Make it VALID — stamp it as approved and correct.

words.definition: To prove that something is genuine, real, or truly what it claims to be.
words.example: An expert was hired to authenticate the painting before the auction house would list it.
words.mnemonic: Make sure it's AUTHENTIC — the real thing, not a knockoff.

words.definition: Able to be believed; trustworthy and convincing.
words.example: Her calm, detailed testimony made her a highly credible witness in the eyes of the jury.
words.mnemonic: Think 'street cred' — from Latin credere, 'to believe'; people believe you.

words.definition: Seeming reasonable or likely to be true, though perhaps not certain.
words.example: He offered a plausible excuse for being late, so his boss let it slide without questions.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'applause' — an idea smooth enough to earn a clap on first hearing.

words.definition: Able to be defended or maintained against attack or objection.
words.example: Once his data was debunked, his position was no longer tenable and he quietly resigned.
words.mnemonic: From Latin tenere, 'to hold' — a stance solid enough to hold onto.

words.definition: False or fake; not genuine despite appearing real or authentic.
words.example: The website spread spurious health claims that had no scientific basis whatsoever.
words.mnemonic: A 'spur'-ious spur looks like a real one but pricks you and leads you astray.

words.definition: Marked by doubt; questionable, uncertain, or not to be trusted.
words.example: The used car had a dubious repair history, so we walked away from the deal.
words.mnemonic: From Latin dubius, 'wavering between two' — like being of 'double' mind, unsure.

words.definition: Seeming true or correct on the surface but actually false or misleading.
words.example: His argument sounded convincing at first, but it was specious and collapsed under scrutiny.
words.mnemonic: From Latin specere, 'to look' — all good looks and shine, nothing real beneath.

words.definition: Based on faulty reasoning or mistaken belief; logically unsound.
words.example: The claim that the moon landing was staged rests on fallacious reasoning at every step.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'fall' inside it — a fallacious argument falls apart because it stands on a fallacy.

words.definition: Clear, logical, and forceful enough to win agreement.
words.example: Her cogent summary of the budget left even the skeptics nodding in agreement.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'co-agent' — a partner whose argument is so tight it forces you to sign on.

words.definition: So powerful or interesting that you cannot look away or disagree.
words.example: The documentary was so compelling that nobody left the theater until the credits ended.
words.mnemonic: COMPEL — it compels you, pulling you in like a magnet you can't resist.

words.definition: Good at making people believe or do something through reasoning or appeal.
words.example: The salesman was so persuasive that I drove home in a car I never planned to buy.
words.mnemonic: 'Per-suede' — a smooth suede glove that gently nudges you toward saying yes.

words.definition: Not final; done cautiously and open to change.
words.example: We made a tentative plan to meet Friday, but nothing is locked in yet.
words.mnemonic: TENT-ative — like a tent, it's easy to fold up and move because nothing is permanent.

words.definition: Settling a question for good, leaving no room for doubt.
words.example: The DNA match was conclusive, so the jury reached a verdict within an hour.
words.mnemonic: Ends on 'close it' — it slams the case shut for the final time.

words.definition: Failing to settle a matter or reach a definite result.
words.example: The blood test came back inconclusive, so the doctor ordered another round of scans.
words.mnemonic: IN- (not) glued onto 'conclusive' — literally 'no conclusion reached.'

words.definition: Based on real observation or experiment rather than pure theory.
words.example: Instead of guessing, she gathered empirical data by measuring each plant every morning.
words.mnemonic: An EMPIRE built brick by measured brick — on tested facts, not fairy tales.

words.definition: Based on personal stories rather than solid data or research.
words.example: The remedy's success is purely anecdotal — a few neighbors swear by it, but no study backs it.
words.mnemonic: 'A neck-dote' — grandma dotes with neck-craning tales at dinner, not statistics.

words.definition: A proposed explanation offered as a starting point for testing.
words.example: Her hypothesis was that sugar speeds plant growth, so she designed an experiment to check it.
words.mnemonic: HYPO (under) + THESIS — an idea placed 'under' the thesis, waiting to be tested.

words.definition: A statement taken as true and used as the base of an argument.
words.example: The whole business plan rests on the premise that shoppers will pay extra for speed.
words.mnemonic: PRE- (before) + MISE (placed) — what you set down before drawing your conclusion.

words.definition: A conclusion reached from evidence and reasoning rather than a direct statement.
words.example: Seeing his muddy boots by the door, she made the inference that he'd cut through the garden.
words.mnemonic: 'Inner-sense' — you sense the answer inside from the clues around you.

words.definition: To reach a conclusion by logical reasoning from known facts.
words.example: From the locked door and the open window, Holmes could deduce how the thief slipped out.
words.mnemonic: DE- (down) + DUCE (lead) — you lead your mind down from facts to the answer.

words.definition: To work out something from clues instead of being told directly.
words.example: From her long silence on the phone, I inferred that she was still upset with me.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'ferre' = to carry — you carry the meaning IN from the clues.

words.definition: To estimate unknown values by extending a known pattern or trend.
words.example: Using this month's sales figures, we can extrapolate what next year's revenue might look like.
words.mnemonic: EXTRA + -polate — you add 'extra' points that reach beyond the edge of your data.

words.definition: To put forward an idea as true, usually to begin an argument.
words.example: The astronomer posits that the planet's rings formed from a shattered moon.
words.mnemonic: Like 'position' — you set your idea firmly into position on the table.

words.definition: To claim or assume that something is true as a starting point for an argument.
words.example: The scientist postulated that a hidden planet was tugging on the comet's orbit.
words.mnemonic: POST-you-late: you POST a claim before the meeting starts and everyone just takes it as given.

words.definition: To state something firmly and confidently as true.
words.example: She asserted her innocence, looking the detective straight in the eye.
words.mnemonic: aSSERT sounds like 'a certainty' — you say it as if it were certain.

words.definition: To claim someone did something wrong, usually without offering proof yet.
words.example: The article alleged that the mayor took bribes, though no charges were ever filed.
words.mnemonic: alLEGE: a LEGAL charge that isn't proven in court yet.

words.definition: To argue strongly that something is the case.
words.example: The lawyer contended that the witness had misremembered the entire evening.
words.mnemonic: conTEND: you TEND your argument like a garden, defending every part of it.

words.definition: To state firmly that something is definitely true.
words.example: He averred, under oath, that he had never met the defendant.
words.mnemonic: aVER: from Latin 'verus' (true) — you swear it's VERy true.

words.definition: To admit, often reluctantly, that something is true or that you have lost.
words.example: After the recount confirmed the result, the candidate finally conceded the election.
words.mnemonic: conCEDE: you CEDE (give up) ground in the debate.

words.definition: A formal statement, often given under oath, about what one saw or knows.
words.example: The bank teller's testimony placed the suspect at the scene that afternoon.
words.mnemonic: TESTImony: a TEST of your honesty, given aloud in court.

words.definition: To confirm or provide evidence that something is true or genuine.
words.example: Anyone who has tasted her cooking can attest to her extraordinary skill.
words.mnemonic: atTEST: you give a TEST-imony that vouches for something.

words.definition: To provide good enough reason for an action to be necessary.
words.example: The strange grinding noise from the engine warranted an immediate stop.
words.mnemonic: WAR-rant: a threat big enough to WARrant taking action.

words.definition: To show that an action or belief is fair, right, or reasonable.
words.example: No excuse could justify leaving the child alone in the locked car.
words.mnemonic: JUST-ify: to make something seem JUST (fair and right).

words.definition: To make an agreement or treaty official by formally approving it.
words.example: The senate voted to ratify the trade treaty late on Thursday night.
words.mnemonic: RATE-ify: the members RATE it good and lock it in as official.

words.definition: To publicly declare your approval or support for someone or something.
words.example: The famous athlete endorsed the new running shoe in every commercial.
words.mnemonic: enDORSE: you sign the back (dorsal side) of a check to approve it.

words.definition: To damage someone's reputation or make their claims seem false.
words.example: The defense tried to discredit the witness by exposing his past lies.
words.mnemonic: DIS-credit: to strip away someone's CREDIT, the trust others place in them.

words.definition: To show that a belief or claim is false or exaggerated.
words.example: The documentary debunked the myth that we use only ten percent of our brains.
words.mnemonic: de-BUNK: to remove the BUNK (nonsense) from an idea.

words.definition: To weaken or damage something gradually and often secretly.
words.example: Constant criticism from his boss slowly undermined his confidence at work.
words.mnemonic: UNDER-mine: digging a MINE UNDER a wall quietly weakens its foundation.

words.definition: To strengthen or give extra support to a position, feeling, or claim.
words.example: The fresh sales figures bolstered her case for opening a second store.
words.mnemonic: A bolster is that long firm pillow that props you up in bed — it holds you steady.

words.definition: To hold up or strengthen an argument, structure, or idea with added support.
words.example: He buttressed his theory with data drawn from three separate studies.
words.mnemonic: Picture a flying buttress — the stone arm that leans in to prop up a cathedral wall.

words.definition: To make something stronger by adding extra material or support.
words.example: Steel bars reinforce the concrete so the bridge can carry heavy trucks.
words.mnemonic: RE + FORCE — you apply force again, adding strength on top of what's there.

words.definition: To form the solid foundation on which something else rests.
words.example: A steady economy underpins the whole country's political stability.
words.mnemonic: UNDER + PIN — a pin placed underneath keeps the entire structure fixed in place.

words.definition: To emphasize or draw special attention to a point.
words.example: The coach underscored the curfew by repeating it three times before the trip.
words.mnemonic: An underscore draws a line beneath a word — you're stressing it, calling it out.

words.definition: To limit or soften a statement by attaching conditions or exceptions.
words.example: She qualified her praise, adding that the report was strong but a week late.
words.mnemonic: You add a 'qualifier' — a condition that narrows and restricts what you just claimed.

words.definition: To avoid committing yourself by giving cautious, noncommittal answers.
words.example: Asked whether he would run, the senator hedged and quickly changed the subject.
words.mnemonic: A hedge is a bush you can hide behind — you duck for cover instead of answering straight.

words.definition: To use vague language on purpose in order to mislead or dodge the truth.
words.example: The witness equivocated, giving replies that could be read two completely different ways.
words.mnemonic: EQUI (equal) + VOC (voice) — two equal voices at once, both saying opposite things.

words.definition: To speak or act evasively so as to hide what is really true.
words.example: Stop prevaricating and tell me exactly where you were last night.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pre-vary' — you keep varying the story rather than give a straight answer.

words.definition: To make something unclear or confusing, usually on purpose.
words.example: The contract's dense jargon obfuscated the fees buried in the fine print.
words.mnemonic: Say it as 'ob-FOG-scate' — you throw fog over the facts so no one can see them.

words.definition: Open to more than one interpretation; not clearly defined.
words.example: Her ambiguous reply left us unsure whether she had agreed or objected.
words.mnemonic: AMBI means 'both' (as in ambidextrous) — it can be taken both ways.

words.definition: Having a doubtful, uncertain meaning that could be taken two ways.
words.example: The test results were equivocal, so the doctor ordered a second scan to be sure.
words.mnemonic: EQUI + VOC — equal voices; the meaning points in two directions at the same time.

words.definition: Leaving no room for doubt; expressed clearly and firmly.
words.example: The board gave an unequivocal yes, with every single member voting in favor.
words.mnemonic: UN (not) glued onto 'equivocal' — the exact opposite of two-way; only one meaning possible.

words.definition: Stated absolutely, without any conditions, hedging, or exceptions.
words.example: He issued a categorical denial, insisting he had never once met the man.
words.mnemonic: Think 'category' — you drop the claim flatly into one box, no maybes allowed.

words.definition: Final, authoritative, and not open to improvement or dispute.
words.example: This biography remains the definitive account; no later book has ever matched it.
words.mnemonic: Shares roots with 'define' and 'final' — it settles the matter once and for all.

words.definition: A statement regarded as obviously true and accepted without requiring any proof.
words.example: In geometry, we begin from the simple axiom that a straight line joins any two points.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ax' + 'I-om' — an idea so sharp it cuts through debate with no proof needed.

words.definition: So obviously true that it needs no proof or further explanation.
words.example: It is axiomatic among chefs that fresh ingredients taste better than stale ones.
words.mnemonic: Axiom + -atic: having the quality of an axiom — a self-evident given.

words.definition: A set of beliefs laid down by an authority as unquestionably true.
words.example: The young professor dared to challenge a dogma that had gone unexamined for decades.
words.mnemonic: 'Dog-ma': a stubborn mom's dog that won't budge — a fixed belief you can't argue with.

words.definition: Asserting beliefs as absolutely true while refusing any argument or doubt.
words.example: He was so dogmatic about his diet that he dismissed every study contradicting it.
words.mnemonic: A 'dog' that 'mad'ly guards one belief and bites anyone who questions it.

words.definition: Following traditional, widely accepted beliefs or established customs.
words.example: Her orthodox approach to teaching relied on textbooks and lectures, never experiments.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'ortho' (correct/straight) + 'dox' (opinion): holding the 'correct,' established opinion.

words.definition: Departing from accepted or traditional beliefs and standards.
words.example: His heterodox economic theories scandalized colleagues who clung to mainstream models.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'hetero' (different) + 'dox' (opinion): holding a different opinion from the accepted one.

words.definition: A principle or belief firmly held by a person or group.
words.example: Nonviolence is a central tenet of the movement he founded.
words.mnemonic: A 'tenet' is what a group holds, like a 'tenant' holds a lease — both from Latin 'tenere,' to hold.

words.definition: A set of principles or teachings held and promoted by a group.
words.example: The military's new doctrine emphasized rapid deployment over sustained occupation.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'doctor' and 'document' — Latin 'docere,' to teach; what the teachers lay down.

words.definition: A rule guiding how one should behave or think.
words.example: She lived by her grandmother's precept: always finish what you start.
words.mnemonic: 'Pre-' (before) + 'cept' (take): a rule you take in beforehand to guide your conduct.

words.definition: Something that naturally follows from an already established fact or proposition.
words.example: Higher rainfall, and as a corollary richer harvests, transformed the valley's economy.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'co-related' — a result that rides along with the main thing already proven.

words.definition: The underlying reasons or logic behind a decision or belief.
words.example: Before voting, the committee asked her to explain the rationale for the budget cuts.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'rational' — the rational thinking that explains why you did something.

words.definition: To assume something is true beforehand as the basis for an argument.
words.example: Your question presupposes that I already agreed to go, which I never did.
words.mnemonic: 'Pre-' (before) + 'suppose': to suppose something in advance, before anything is proven.

words.definition: Something believed to be true in advance without full proof.
words.example: The legal system rests on the presumption that the accused is innocent until proven guilty.
words.mnemonic: 'Pre-' (before) + 'sume' (take): an idea you take to be true before the facts arrive.

words.definition: An opinion or conclusion formed from incomplete information or guesswork.
words.example: Without any hard data, the detective's theory was pure conjecture.
words.mnemonic: 'Con-' (together) + 'jecture' (throw, as in 'project'): you throw ideas together into a guess.

words.definition: To guess or conclude something using little evidence.
words.example: From the muddy boots by the door, she surmised he'd been walking in the fields.
words.mnemonic: 'Sir, my eyes' — using only what your eyes catch to guess the rest.

words.definition: To form theories or guesses about a matter without firm evidence.
words.example: Analysts began to speculate about who would run the company once the CEO resigned.
words.mnemonic: 'Spec' like spectacles — you peer through foggy glasses at possibilities you can't yet see clearly.

words.definition: To propose a tentative explanation as a starting point for further investigation.
words.example: The scientist hypothesized that the plants grew faster under blue light and set up a test.
words.mnemonic: 'Hypo' = under + 'thesis' = a placing: an idea placed underneath, waiting to be tested.

words.definition: A logical argument that draws a conclusion from two stated premises.
words.example: "All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal" is the classic syllogism.
words.mnemonic: Say it slowly: syl-LOGIC-ism — logic sits right in the middle of the word.

words.definition: Clever but deliberately misleading reasoning meant to deceive.
words.example: His speech sounded airtight, but it was pure sophistry designed to dodge the real question.
words.mnemonic: So-FIST-ry: a sneaky ancient Sophist punching holes in truth with fake logic.

words.definition: The art of using language persuasively in speech or writing.
words.example: The senator's soaring rhetoric stirred the crowd but offered few concrete plans.
words.mnemonic: A 'rhetor' was the ancient Greek orator — picture him roaring to sway the crowd.

words.definition: A forceful spoken or written attack on an opinion or position.
words.example: Her polemic against factory farming pulled no punches and named names.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'polemos' = war — a polemic is a war of words. Sounds like 'PUMMEL-ick.'

words.definition: A long, formal written work that examines a subject systematically.
words.example: He spent a decade writing a treatise on the history of monetary policy.
words.mnemonic: It 'treats' a topic exhaustively — a treat-ISE served up for scholars.

words.definition: Extended, serious communication about a topic, spoken or written.
words.example: The panel elevated the public discourse on climate policy far above the usual shouting.
words.mnemonic: 'This course' of talk runs on and on, coursing steadily through the subject.

words.definition: A clear, detailed explanation of an idea or theory.
words.example: Her exposition of quantum theory made the strange ideas surprisingly easy to follow.
words.mnemonic: Ex + pose = to set out in the open; it exposes the meaning for all to see.

words.definition: To make something clear by explaining it plainly.
words.example: Could you elucidate the second step? I still don't see how you got the answer.
words.mnemonic: e-LUCID-ate: LUCID means clear, from Latin 'lux' (light) — you shed light on it.

words.definition: To set out and explain something in careful detail.
words.example: The professor loved to expound on medieval trade routes for hours at a stretch.
words.mnemonic: Ex + pound: you pound OUT your points one by one until nothing is left unsaid.

words.definition: To analyze an idea or text and develop its meaning in detail.
words.example: The critic explicated the poem line by line, unpacking every buried image.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'plicare' = to fold; to ex-plicate is to unfold the meaning — same root as 'explicit.'

words.definition: To describe or mark out something precisely.
words.example: The contract delineates each partner's duties down to the smallest task.
words.mnemonic: de-LINE-ate: draw the LINES around something to show exactly where its edges fall.

words.definition: To express thoughts clearly and effectively in words.
words.example: She articulated her objections so well that the board reversed its decision on the spot.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'articulus' = a joint; you join your words neatly, like well-fitted bones.

words.definition: To name or list things one by one.
words.example: The auditor enumerated every expense, from paperclips to transatlantic airfare.
words.mnemonic: e-NUMER-ate: a NUMBER hides inside — you number the items off, one after another.
